result: The authors generated a complete connectome of all 20 hugin-producing neurons in the Drosophila larval CNS using serial section electron microscopy (ssTEM), demonstrating that neurons of the same class have very similar distributions of pre- and postsynaptic sites.
evaluation: Claims C3, C36, and C37 describe the primary methodological achievement and a key observation. The EM-based reconstruction is clearly documented in the methods and figures, and the similarity in synaptic site distribution within classes is shown in Figure 2C-E and Video 1, providing strong visual and quantitative support.

result: Hugin-PC and hugin-VNC interneurons use acetylcholine as a neurotransmitter in addition to the hugin neuropeptide, as evidenced by the presence of small clear core vesicles (SCVs) at presynaptic sites and expression of choline acetyltransferase (ChAT).
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C43, C44, C49, C50, and C51 collectively demonstrate dual transmission. The presence of SCVs at presynaptic sites (C43, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C) provides ultrastructural evidence, while ChAT immunoreactivity and promoter expression (C49, C50, Figure 3A,B) provide molecular confirmation. The consistency across multiple independent methods strongly supports this conclusion.

result: Both hugin neuropeptide and acetylcholine are necessary for the regulatory effect of hugin neurons on feeding behavior, as demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments that rescue feeding suppression phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C6, C52, C53, C54, and C56 describe functional validation experiments. The RNAi knockdown of either hugin neuropeptide or ChAT rescues both food intake and pharyngeal pumping phenotypes (Figure 3C,D), with appropriate controls (LacZ RNAi). The convergent rescue by independent knockdowns provides strong evidence that both transmitters are required.

result: Each hugin neuron class forms a distinct microcircuit with reciprocal within-class connections and unique sets of synaptic partners, with minimal overlap between classes.
evaluation: Claims C57-C61 and C66 describe the organizational principle of hugin connectivity. The reciprocal connections within classes (C57, Figure 4), shared synaptic partners within but not between classes (C59, C60, Figure 5B), and spatial segregation of partners (C61, Figure 5C, Video 2) are all well-documented in the connectomic data. The quantitative connectivity similarity analysis supports the conclusion of distinct microcircuits.

result: Hugin neurons receive substantial chemosensory input in the SEZ, with 68 afferent neurons identified that cluster into seven groups based on synapse similarity, providing up to 39% of incoming connections to hugin-PC and hugin-VNC neurons.
evaluation: Claims C67, C69-C73, and C82 describe the sensory input architecture. The identification of 68 afferent neurons (C69, Figure 6A), their clustering into seven groups (C72, Figure 6B, Video 3), and the quantification of their contribution to hugin neuron inputs (C67, C82) are all supported by the connectomic reconstruction. The synapse similarity score clustering method is described in Materials and methods.

result: Sensory inputs to hugin neurons include gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) from the antennal nerve but not olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs), with activation of hugin-PC neurons by bitter stimuli likely based on monosynaptic connections to GRNs.
evaluation: Claims C74-C77 and C84 characterize the sensory modality of inputs. The anatomical identification of GRNs and ORNs in the antennal nerve (C74, C75, Figure 6C,D) is supported by citations. The absence of ORN inputs (C76, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and morphological identification of GRNs (C77) are documented in the connectomic data. The inference about monosynaptic connections (C84) is reasonable given the direct connections observed and prior functional data (C83).

result: Hugin-PC neurons make extensive synaptic contacts onto median neurosecretory cells (mNSCs) in the pars intercerebralis, with connectivity-based clustering identifying three groups corresponding to DH44-, DMS-, and insulin-producing cells, with primary targeting of insulin-producing cells.
evaluation: Claims C86-C94 describe the neuroendocrine connectivity. The synaptic contacts onto mNSCs (C88, Figure 7B) and the clustering analysis (C90, Figure 7D) are well-documented. The inference of mNSC identities (C91-C93) based on clustering matching known cell numbers is reasonable, though indirect. The preferential targeting of insulin-producing cells (C94) is supported by the connectivity matrix. The homology to mammalian hypothalamus (C86) is supported by citation.

result: The hugin receptor PK2-R1 (CG8784) is expressed in all three types of mNSCs, and application of hugin neuropeptide increases calcium activity in mNSCs, demonstrating that hugin-PC neurons employ both synaptic and peptidergic signaling to target the neuroendocrine center.
evaluation: Claims C100-C107 establish the peptidergic signaling pathway. The generation of CG8784-GAL4 lines (C102, Figure 8A) and co-localization with all three mNSC types (C103-C105, Figure 8B-D) provide molecular evidence for receptor expression. The calcium imaging experiments (C106, Figure 8—figure supplement 2) provide functional validation. Together with the synaptic connectivity data, this supports the dual signaling mechanism (C107).

result: Dense core vesicles (DCVs) in hugin-PC and hugin-VNC neurons localize close to but not exclusively at presynaptic sites, with 98% of hugin-PC to mNSC synapses having nearby DCVs, suggesting both synaptic co-release and para-/non-synaptic release of neuropeptide.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 describe the spatial relationship between DCVs and synapses. The EM observations (C108, Figure 9A,B) and quantification at hugin-PC to mNSC synapses (C109, Figure 9C) are clearly documented. The interpretation of para- and non-synaptic release (C110) is supported by the observation that most DCVs are distant from synapses and by citations to relevant literature.

result: Hugin neurons in Drosophila and NeuromedinU neurons in mammals represent an ancient, conserved physiological control system, with functional and molecular parallels including homologous downstream targets (DH44/CRH and insulin-like peptides) and similar roles in feeding and activity regulation.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C10, C11, C20, C140, C141, and C144 propose evolutionary conservation. While the functional similarities (C1, C2) and homology of downstream targets (C10, C141) are supported by citations, the proposal of an ancient conserved system (C11, C144) and the specific homology of hugin to central NMU (C140) are speculative interpretations. The comparative analysis is compelling but lacks direct evolutionary evidence or detailed characterization of mammalian NMU connectivity to fully support the conservation claim.

result: Efferent hugin neurons (hugin-RG and hugin-PH) show essentially no presynaptic sites or small clear core vesicles within the CNS, with hugin-RG neurons having membrane specializations at the ring gland that border haemal space, indicating neuroendocrine release.
evaluation: Claims C38-C42 characterize efferent hugin neurons. The absence of presynaptic sites and SCVs (C38, C39) and the presence of membrane specializations with DCVs at the ring gland (C40, C41) are documented in the EM data. The interpretation of neuroendocrine release (C42, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) is reasonable based on the ultrastructural features and location bordering haemal space.

result: Hugin-PC and hugin-VNC neurons have mixed input-output compartments with both pre- and postsynaptic sites along their neurites, with all hugin neurons receiving inputs in the SEZ but only hugin-PC showing considerable synaptic outputs there.
evaluation: Claims C45, C46, and C48 describe the synaptic organization of hugin interneurons. The mixed input-output compartments (C45, Figure 2D,E) and the distribution of inputs and outputs (C46, C48) are clearly shown in the EM reconstruction data. The consistency with prior functional studies (C48, citations) provides additional support.

result: Different groups of sensory neurons show selective connectivity to specific hugin classes, with groups 2-5 connecting almost exclusively to hugin-PC, group 7 primarily to hugin-VNC, and group 1 to both hugin-PC and hugin-VNC.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 describe the specificity of sensory-to-hugin connectivity. The selective connectivity patterns (Figure 6E) are documented in the connectomic reconstruction and are consistent with the clustering analysis. The quantitative data support the differential targeting of hugin classes by sensory neuron groups.

result: Synapses between hugin-PC neurons and mNSCs constitute a large fraction of their respective connections (up to 35% for hugin-PC, up to 17% for mNSCs), with most presynaptic partners of hugin-PC also connecting to mNSCs, demonstrating that the neuroendocrine system is a major target of hugin neurons.
evaluation: Claims C95-C99 quantify the hugin-PC to mNSC connectivity. The percentages (C96, C97) are stated in the text and the shared presynaptic partners (C98, Figure 7E) are documented in the connectomic data. The prior finding of muscarinic ACh receptor expression in IPCs (C95) is supported by citation. Together, these support the conclusion that the neuroendocrine system is a major target (C99).

result: The vast majority of synapses for hugin-RG (93±4%) and hugin-PH (97±3%) are with interneurons, with lower percentages for hugin-PC (66±6%) and hugin-VNC (81±2%).
evaluation: Claims C62-C65 provide quantitative characterization of synaptic partner types. These percentages are stated in the text and are derived from the connectomic reconstruction. The data support the conclusion that efferent hugin neurons primarily connect to interneurons within the CNS, while hugin-PC and hugin-VNC have more diverse targets.

result: Multiple hormonal and neuropeptide systems show functional conservation between mammals and Drosophila, including insulin, glucagon, leptin, and NMU/hugin, with NMU widely distributed in mammalian CNS regions including hypothalamus, pituitary, brainstem, and spinal cord.
evaluation: Claims C12-C18 and C21-C26 establish the context of conserved metabolic signaling systems. These are all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. The claims about NMU distribution (C23-C26) and function (C15-C18) in mammals, and hugin function in Drosophila (C21, C22), provide the comparative framework for the study. The molecular classification of hugin (C19) is established knowledge.

result: While the number and morphology of NMU-producing neurons in mammals is unknown, hugin in Drosophila is expressed in only 20 neurons in the CNS that can be classified into four morphological classes based on projection targets: hugin-PC (8 neurons), hugin-VNC (4 neurons), hugin-RG (4 neurons), and hugin-PH (4 neurons).
evaluation: Claims C27-C35 establish the anatomical organization of hugin neurons. The statement about unknown mammalian NMU neuron numbers (C27) highlights a knowledge gap. The classification of hugin neurons (C32-C35) is well-established in prior literature (citations provided) and confirmed by the current EM reconstruction (Figure 2A). The distribution of hugin peptide (C28-C31) is supported by citation and Figure 1.

result: Different hugin classes have distinct functions, with hugin-PC neurons decreasing food intake and processing aversive gustatory cues, and hugin-VNC neurons increasing locomotion without affecting food intake. Each class forms independent microcircuits suggesting distinct functional contexts.
evaluation: Claims C83, C113, C114 describe prior functional characterization (supported by citations), while C115 and C116 present new interpretations based on the connectomic data. The observation of independent microcircuits (C115) is well-supported by the connectivity analysis. The prediction of distinct functional contexts (C116) is a reasonable inference from the connectivity data, though it remains to be experimentally validated. The integrative function of hugin-PC (C85) is a reasonable speculation based on the diversity of sensory inputs.

result: Co-transmission of neuropeptides and small molecule transmitters is widespread across species, with various examples in mammals and invertebrates showing different patterns of target specificity and activity-dependent release, providing context for understanding hugin neuron function.
evaluation: Claims C111, C112, C123-C129 provide comparative context from the literature on co-transmission. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior studies in mammals (C111, C112, C123, C124), frogs (C125), and Aplysia (C126, C128, C129). The general principle about activity-dependent release (C127) is also citation-supported. These establish the broader context for interpreting the hugin findings.

result: Insulin-producing cells centrally regulate feeding behavior in Drosophila, and hugin neuron morphology and function appear conserved between larval and adult stages, with hugin neurons acting as a brake on feeding behavior in both stages.
evaluation: Claims C117, C118 establish the role of IPCs in feeding regulation (supported by citations). Claims C119-C122 discuss conservation across developmental stages, all supported by citations to prior work. These claims provide context for understanding the significance of hugin-PC connections to IPCs and support the interpretation that the larval connectome may be relevant to adult function.

result: NMU and its receptors (NMUR1 and NMUR2) have distinct distributions and functions in mammals, with parallels to Drosophila systems including Limostatin as a peripheral NMU homolog. Neuroendocrine centers and their connections to sensory systems show evolutionary conservation across species.
evaluation: Claims C130-C139 and C142-C146 provide extensive comparative context from the mammalian and evolutionary literature. All claims are supported by appropriate citations. The discussion of NMU receptor distribution and function (C131-C134, C137-C139), the Limostatin parallel (C135, C136), and evolutionary conservation (C142, C143, C145, C146) establish the broader significance of the hugin findings and support the comparative framework of the study.
